source: Jentzsch & Kersting (2023) ChatGPT is fun, but it is not funny
finding: ChatGPT's jokes are mostly a tiny fixed set, not newly made. It explains real jokes well but invents explanations for non-jokes, and judges jokes by surface form.
numbers: 1008 generated jokes; over 90% were the same 25 jokes; top 4 jokes were over 50%. For 23 of 25 valid jokes the explanation was valid. In detection, jokes with two characteristics removed were all classed as no joke (25 of 25 per set).
limits: ChatGPT (early 2023) only; 25-joke samples; exploratory; no human control group.
agent_relevance: A model asked to be funny returns memorised templates. An agent needs a novelty check against known outputs, not self-judgement.

source: Gomez-Rodriguez & Williams (2023) A Confederacy of Models: LLMs on Creative Writing
finding: GPT-4 beat human writers overall and on 8 of 10 rubric items. Humans kept the lead on originality. Humor split models into two groups: ones that could do it and ones that failed.
numbers: 12 LLMs x 5 stories = 60 stories plus 5 human stories (creative-writing students); one prompt (Ignatius J. Reilly vs a pterodactyl). Humor was the hardest item, mean 3.4 of 10; Claude best on dark humor, humans close second.
limits: Only 5 human stories; small rater pool; 2023 models; humans were students, not professionals.
agent_relevance: Models differ a lot on creative axes. Rate originality and humor separately, never as one score.

source: Chakrabarty, Laban, Agarwal, Muresan, Wu (2024) Art or Artifice? LLMs and the False Promise of Creativity (TTCW)
finding: On 14 Torrance-style binary tests, expert-rated LLM stories passed 3 to 10 times fewer tests than New Yorker stories. LLMs used as judges did not agree with experts.
numbers: 10 writers rated 48 stories. Expert agreement moderate per test; aggregate Pearson 0.69. Professional stories passed 84.7% of tests; LLM stories passed from about 9% (ChatGPT) up to 30% (Claude). LLM assessor correlations with experts were close to zero.
limits: Short stories only; small expert panel; 2023 models (GPT-3.5/4, Claude 1.3).
agent_relevance: An LLM judge of creativity is near-useless. The schema should not let the model grade creative quality without an external check.

source: Hessel et al. (2023) Do Androids Laugh at Electric Sheep? New Yorker Caption Contest benchmarks
finding: Models were far worse than humans at matching jokes to cartoons, ranking winning captions and explaining jokes. A written scene description helped language-only models.
numbers: Best multimodal model (fine-tuned CLIP ViT-L/14) reached 62% on a 5-way match task; humans 94%. Human explanations beat the best machine explanations in 87.8% of pairs. At equal supervision GPT-4 explanations were preferred in 93% of pairs over the weaker setup.
limits: 2022-23 models; scene descriptions were hand-annotated; crowd judges.
agent_relevance: Task structure (a written description step) matters more than model size.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Humor in AI: Massive Scale Crowd-Sourced Preferences and Cartoon Captioning
finding: GPT-4o and Claude-3-Opus still lose to top human captions. RLHF and DPO fine-tuning barely helped; PPO training moved the wrong way against human contestants.
numbers: Dataset: over 250 million ratings on 2.2 million captions. On 91 held-out cartoons, Claude-3-Opus overall win rate 54.4% vs human top-10 captions, GPT-4o 44.5% (GPT judge). Claude captions were preferred over human top-10 by only 1.6% (humor expert) and 35.4% (crowd workers).
limits: Main table judged by GPT-4; human check was 6 workers plus one expert.
agent_relevance: 1.6% vs 35.4% shows the judge changes the verdict. Use expert-like or ground-truth checks.

source: Mirowski, Mathewson, Pittman, Evans (2023) Co-Writing Screenplays and Theatre Scripts with Language Models (Dramatron)
finding: Dramatron chains prompts hierarchically (log line, title, characters, plot beats, locations, dialogue) to get long coherent scripts. 15 professionals found it useful for ideas and drafts, not as a finished writer.
numbers: 15 theatre and film professionals; scripts staged at the Edmonton International Fringe; interviews raised plagiarism and bias concerns.
limits: Qualitative; no controlled baseline; Chinchilla-class model.
agent_relevance: Modern descendant of TALE-SPIN planning: a hierarchical plan with code-controlled order. Fits our rule that the program decides and the model fills a slot.

source: Mirowski, Love, Mathewson, Mohamed (2024) A Robot Walks into a Bar: LLMs as creativity support tools for comedy
finding: 20 professional comedians judged LLMs weak as comedy tools: bland, biased tropes. Safety filters erased minority perspectives, which they called censorship.
numbers: 20 comedians, 3-hour workshops (Edinburgh Fringe Aug 2023 and online), Creativity Support Index plus focus groups. Quote: 'cruise ship comedy material from the 1950s, but a bit less racist'.
limits: Small, self-selected AI-using comedians; 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Alignment tuning narrows humor. Creative operators may need a less filtered draft step.

source: Yang, Tian, Peng, Klein (2022) Re3: Generating Longer Stories With Recursive Reprompting and Revision
finding: A Plan, Draft, Rewrite, Edit loop around GPT-3 gave more coherent, premise-relevant stories. Plan and Rewrite mattered; Edit did little.
numbers: Vs rolling-window baseline: coherent 60.0 vs 45.7%, relevant 64.0 vs 44.0%, interesting 54.3 vs 45.0%, judged human 83.3 vs 74.0%. Vs fine-tuned baseline: coherent 60.0 vs 48.7%, relevant 65.3 vs 49.3%.
limits: GPT-3 175B era; stories over 2000 words; rerank step uses model scoring; contradiction detector only moderate ROC-AUC.
agent_relevance: A tested generate-rank-revise scaffold. The Rewrite step is best-of-N with a coherence check.

source: Tian et al. (2024) Are LLMs Capable of Generating Human-Level Narratives?
finding: LLM stories are homogeneously positive, put turning points early and lack tension. Adding story-arc or turning-point information to the prompt improved diversity and suspense.
numbers: Diversity up 45% with arc-aware prompting; suspense and engagement up 40% with turning-point guidance. Climax and setback turning points appear in 14.6% and 9.3% of human stories, GPT-4 only 1.3% and 1.7%.
limits: GPT-4 and open models of 2024; gains relative to vanilla prompts.
agent_relevance: Concrete prompt scaffold with measured gains: inject explicit discourse structure.

source: Huot et al. (2025) Agents' Room: Narrative Generation through Multi-Step Collaboration
finding: Specialised writing agents guided by a plan beat end-to-end and two-stage baselines for expert raters, but human-written stories were still preferred on every dimension.
numbers: Raters preferred the longer story only 0.51 of the time, so length is not the driver. The LLM judge repeats its own choice 90.2% of the time in a second run.
limits: Gap smaller for language use than for plot and ideas; LLM judge agreement with humans only moderate.
agent_relevance: Decomposition into specialised roles helps but does not close the gap.

source: Franceschelli & Musolesi (2024) On the Creativity of Large Language Models
finding: Review applying Boden's value, novelty and surprise to LLMs; covers product, process, press and person views and lists easy and hard problems of machine creativity.
numbers: No experiments; conceptual analysis.
limits: Position paper; no measured results.
agent_relevance: Vocabulary for why LLM output is mostly combinational or exploratory, not transformational.

source: Horvitz et al. (2024) Getting Serious about Humor: Crafting Humor Datasets with Unfunny LLMs
finding: LLMs are good at removing humor (unfun-ing) but weak at making it. Detectors trained on GPT-4 unfun data score about as well as on human-edited data.
numbers: Detector holdout accuracy: GPT-4 unfun 99%, GPT-3.5 98%, human unfun 92%. All synthetic humor rated significantly less funny than Onion headlines (p<0.05); no significant GPT-3.5 vs GPT-4 gain. English-Hindi: GPT-4 edited text rated humorous 3.6% (filtered) vs 48% for original humorous tweets.
limits: Headline domain; n=100 per approach; 10 annotators.
agent_relevance: Editing out humor is easy; making it is hard. Edit-based creation (transform an existing joke) may beat from-scratch generation.

source: Xu et al. (2024) A good pun is its own reword: Can LLMs understand puns?
finding: GPT-4-Turbo and Claude-3-Opus rival older specialised pun systems on success rate but fall into 'lazy pun generation' patterns and are weaker on heterographic puns. Chain-of-thought improved recognition accuracy.
numbers: Prior state of the art (Tian 2022) success rate 56% homographic and 47% heterographic; GPT-4-Turbo and Claude-3-Opus rival it. Their puns are still judged less funny than human puns.
limits: Open 7B models far weaker; success rate is not funniness.
agent_relevance: Direct comparison with JAPE-style rule systems: LLMs match them on mechanical success but not on funniness.

source: Wenger & Kenett (2025) We're Different, We're the Same: Creative Homogeneity Across LLMs
finding: Across about a dozen LLMs, responses to creativity tests were much more similar to each other than human responses are to each other.
numbers: Population variability (cosine distance), LLM vs human: AUT 0.459 vs 0.738 (effect 2.2), FF 0.534 vs 0.835 (2.0), DAT 0.665 vs 0.819 (1.4). Individual originality was close (AUT 0.711 vs 0.696).
limits: Divergent-thinking tests, not stories or jokes; default system prompt.
agent_relevance: Sampling the same model, or several models, gives correlated creativity. Diversity must come from structured variation, not model choice.

source: Oogiri study (2025) Assessing LLMs in Humor: Multi-dimensional Analysis of Oogiri Generation and Evaluation
finding: GPT-4.1, Gemini 2.5 Pro and Claude Sonnet 4 wrote Oogiri answers at the level of low to mid-tier humans, weakest on Empathy. LLM judges agree only weakly with humans and weight Novelty where humans weight Empathy.
numbers: Six dimensions, 5-point human ratings; Gemini 2.5 Pro best generator; Claude Sonnet 4 had the highest correlation with humans among judges, but overall agreement limited.
limits: Japanese humor; few models; moderate correlations.
agent_relevance: LLM judges have their own taste. For humor, use counted checks, not a funniness score.

source: HumorRank (2026) Tournament-based leaderboard for humor generation
finding: Pairwise LLM judges using General Theory of Verbal Humor tags rank nine models; rankings are stable across judges; small fine-tuned models can match much larger ones.
numbers: Kendall tau 0.889 between Llama 3.3 70B and Qwen 2.5 72B judge rankings on both benchmarks; human-LLM agreement tracks human-human agreement on hard pairs.
limits: Automated judging; two benchmarks (SemEval-2026 MWAHAHA, Humor Transfer Bench); stability is not validity.
agent_relevance: Pairwise tournaments with a theory-based rubric are more stable than absolute scores and can be counted by the program.

source: COMIC (2026) Agentic Sketch Comedy Generation
finding: A population of role agents with critics aligned to YouTube viewer preferences, plus island evolution of scripts, beat video-model and agent baselines in human and automatic evaluation.
numbers: Win rate (single-best critic): COMIC 0.44, No-Refine 0.30, MovieAgent 0.02, VGoT 0.03; channel-wise best critic 0.39, 0.31, 0.13, 0.17. Win rate rose sharply through generation 4. Ordering COMIC > Sora > Veo > MovieAgent > VGoT.
limits: Win rates are within pools, not absolute funniness; critics tuned on YouTube comedy.
agent_relevance: A closed-loop evolutionary search with learned critics works for humor; links to quality-diversity (subfield 06).

source: Spotting the Artificial (2026) Dialogic humor improvisation in humans and LLMs
finding: Multi-agent LLM improv scenes were coherent but too polite and positive, and missed features of spontaneous spoken interaction.
numbers: Automated linguistic measures plus manual Systemic Functional Linguistics annotation; no single headline number.
limits: Small corpora; analysis rather than a benchmark.
agent_relevance: Same positivity bias as in story arcs (Tian 2024); creative role-play should be prompted for conflict.

source: StoryWriter (2025) A Multi-Agent Framework for Long Story Generation
finding: Outline, planning and writing agents with a sliding window over story history beat LongWriter and GPT-4o on long stories.
numbers: Better story quality and length in human and automated evaluation across length bands [0,4k) to [10k,20k) words (MoPS); exact percentages not extracted.
limits: GLM and Llama backbones; numbers not recorded.
agent_relevance: Another planner-writer split with history compression; supports a bounded-context writer slot.

source: Wikipedia (2025) AARON (Harold Cohen)
finding: AARON ran 1972 to the 2010s on hand-coded drawing rules, later colour. It cannot learn new styles; every capability was coded by Cohen. Output follows a noticeable formula.
numbers: Moved from C to Lisp in the early 1990s; Kurzweil released a screensaver version.
limits: Secondary source; no controlled audience test cited.
agent_relevance: Fixed rules give endless but same-style output, like one fixed prompt template.

source: Wikipedia (2025) Computational humor: JAPE and STANDUP
finding: JAPE (Binsted and Ritchie, 1994) made riddle puns from a general lexicon using templates. STANDUP (2007) was tested with children with communication disabilities and showed improvement on some language tests.
numbers: Examples: 'A bizarre bazaar'. First dedicated conference 1996.
limits: Wikipedia summary; original evaluation numbers not opened.
agent_relevance: Rule-based pun templates still compete with LLMs on success rate (see c13).

source: Wikipedia (2025) Experiments in Musical Intelligence (David Cope)
finding: EMI recombines patterns from a composer's music. In Hofstadter's lecture, audiences did no better than chance at telling real Chopin from EMI Chopin-style.
numbers: About 20,000 lines of Lisp (2001); 5,000 Bach-style MIDI pieces published; Cope deleted the database in 2005.
limits: No listener counts on the page; the test was informal.
agent_relevance: Style recombination can fool listeners; the critique is lack of novelty, as with LLM style imitation.

source: Porter & Machery (2024) AI-generated poetry is indistinguishable from human-written poetry and is rated more favorably
finding: Non-expert readers could not tell ChatGPT-3.5 poems in famous poets' styles from the originals and rated AI poems higher, until told they were AI.
numbers: Study 1: 1,634 participants, 46.6% correct (below chance). Study 2: 696 participants; AI poems rated higher on rhythm and beauty; AI-labelled poems rated lower on 13 traits.
limits: Known from abstract and press coverage only, not the full paper; non-expert raters.
agent_relevance: Lay preference follows simplicity and the label. Lay ratings are weak evidence of quality.

source: Meehan (1976) The Metanovel: Writing Stories by Computer (TALE-SPIN)
finding: TALE-SPIN planned stories by giving characters goals and simulating their plan steps. It is known for mis-spun tales where the simulated world made the story pointless.
numbers: No numbers recorded; recalled from background knowledge.
limits: Not opened this session; details are recalled, not verified.
agent_relevance: Ancestor of Dramatron-style planning: a correct simulation is not a good story.

source: Turner (1994) The Creative Process: A Computer Model of Storytelling (MINSTREL)
finding: MINSTREL wrote King Arthur tales by transform-recall-adapt (TRAMs): retrieve a known story, transform its problem, adapt the result. Creativity came from case-based analogy.
numbers: No numbers recorded; recalled from background knowledge.
limits: Not opened this session; recalled only.
agent_relevance: TRAMs are an analogy operator that could be prompted: retrieve a prior case, mutate it, check it.
